title: What Is Going On Inside?
reflection: Think of one small, ordinary flashpoint at home. What might your child’s mind have needed in the minute before it?

questions.q: When a child’s behaviour puzzles a parent, which question does Lesson 2 ask first?
o: What consequence will make clear to the child that this is not acceptable?
What is wrong with this child, and how soon can it be put right?
What set this off, so that it can be taken out of the child’s day?
Which need might be missing: rest, food, quiet, closeness or feeling safe?
questions.e: Behaviour is very often the whistle: the meltdown, the “attitude”, the silence, the lie. What is happening underneath is what the child’s mind needs right now. When behaviour puzzles us, we can ask which basic need might be missing before we ask what is wrong with the child.
questions.c: Behaviour is the kettle’s whistle: ask what the mind needs, not why

questions.q: A four-year-old lies on the supermarket floor at half past five, screaming after being refused a biscuit. Which response fits Lesson 2?
o: Give the biscuit, so that the storm ends and everyone can get home.
Say the limit firmly at once, so that he learns straight away that the answer will not change.
Get close, lower the voice and steady him, and give the limit once the storm has passed.
Wait nearby without a word until he stops, so that the tantrum earns him nothing.
questions.e: Two moves, and the order matters: first steady, then steer. Steady the child by getting close, lowering your voice, perhaps picking him up. When the storm has passed, steer: “We don’t lie on the floor, and the biscuit is not for today.” A limit given to a mind in full whistle mostly bounces off.

questions.q: “Once a child is flat on the floor, a parent can help just as easily as in the minute before the storm began.”
questions.e: A big feeling is rarely one event. It is the loop going round again, a little stronger each time. The cheapest place to help is early, while the ripple is small. By the time “me” has claimed it and memory has joined in, it is a storm.
questions.c: The cheapest place to help is early in the loop, while the ripple is small

questions.q: After a stormy hour, a parent wants to describe a twelve-year-old’s mood to him. Which sentence fits Lesson 2?
o: “You are such an angry boy lately.”
“You are having a very angry afternoon.”
“You have a temper, and we need to work on it.”
“You are fine, and there is nothing to be upset about.”
questions.e: Worry, anger and shyness are states of the inner instrument, and the child is the awareness in which they appear. Clouds are real, but they are not the sky. It changes the sentence we say: not “you are so angry” but “you are having a very angry afternoon.”
questions.c: The state a child is in is weather, not who they are

questions.q: In the lesson’s picture of the mind as an office, what accounts for a young child who feels everything yet cannot decide what to do with it?
o: Reception is slow, so what comes in reaches the child late and in a rush.
The filing room is empty, so nothing yet shapes how the child responds.
The name badge has not yet started work, so the child cannot tell me apart from not-me at all.
The manager, who settles what things mean and what to do, is new and has a small desk.
questions.e: Reception is working at full speed, the name badge is already stamping “mine” on everything within reach, but the manager is only just learning the job. The lesson offers this as a model for understanding, not a developmental fact. A young child can feel everything and cannot yet decide what to do with it.
questions.c: The inner office: a young child’s manager is new

questions.q: A five-year-old is upset because a promised outing has been cancelled, and cannot decide what to do instead. Which response fits the idea of lending the child your manager?
o: Choose an activity firmly for him, so that the upset ends quickly.
Name the feeling, offer two simple choices, and give a little time.
Leave him to sort it out alone, since that is how his manager will grow.
Explain at length why the outing could not happen and what is possible instead.
questions.e: When a child cannot yet decide, you decide with them, gently. Name the feeling: “That was really disappointing.” Offer two choices. Give a little time. You are doing for them what their manager will one day do for itself.
questions.c: Lend your child your manager: name the feeling, offer two choices

questions.q: “In the picture of the chariot, the senses are the trouble, and a parent’s task is to keep a child from being pulled toward whatever the senses find interesting.”
questions.e: The horses are not the problem. The senses are not bad. They need steering. When the mind is steady and understanding is clear, the same senses become like good horses. A parent steadies the cart for a while, until the child can steer.
questions.c: The horses need steering, not shouting at

questions.q: A seven-year-old, absorbed in looking at the wall, has not put his shoes on after being asked twice. Which approach fits Lesson 2?
o: Raise the voice, so that the instruction cuts through whatever he is absorbed in.
Say it three ways, so that at least one of the ways is sure to reach him.
Stand beside him at his level until you have his eyes, say one thing, and wait.
Tell him that the shoes must be on within a minute, or something will be lost.
questions.e: A mind absorbed in something has its attention fully held, and the reins are not on you. Stand beside him, at his level, until you have his eyes. Say one thing, not three. Wait a moment.
questions.c: Steady attention first: one thing, at the child’s level, then wait

questions.q: What does Lesson 2 say about when parenting begins?
o: At birth, when care for the child and teaching of the child can begin together.
In pregnancy, when a mother’s calm or distress shapes how the child will turn out.
It can begin as welcome, even before a child arrives, and is never too late to offer.
Only for those who prepared with care and calm well before the child was conceived.
questions.e: Parenting can begin as hospitality, long before it becomes instruction. Resonance is not a judgement on a family or on a child, however they came. Some pregnancies were not planned, some children arrive by adoption or fostering, and the welcome begins whenever the child arrives. It is never too late to offer it.
questions.c: Parenting as welcome, not a test, from whenever the child arrives

questions.q: A parent whose child is struggling asks, “Did I fail to prepare?” Which reply fits Lesson 2?
o: Nothing that happens before birth can matter at all, so she has nothing to wonder about or to feel.
Preparation is welcome, not a test, and a struggling child is no proof that anyone failed.
The early months do matter, so she should now work harder to make up for them.
Looking back over the pregnancy for what went wrong would let her do better next time.
questions.e: That would be a misuse of the idea. Resonance is not a judgement on a family or on a child. A child who struggles is no proof that anyone failed. Preparation is welcome, not a test, and the welcome can be offered at any age.
questions.c: Preparation is welcome, not a test; a struggling child is no proof anyone failed
